doc.title: Carmen Lundy interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 15, 2023

title: Double major at Miami and learning classmates' original songs
summary: Classical voice plus jazz courses with Jerry Coker's department; she effectively started the jazz vocal path and learned classmates' new songs.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: year of school. And I’m in this classical department and I’m doing all of the arias and I’m learning all this stuff and it was great because I got wonderful vocal instruction that has allowed me to sustain a fifty year career so thank you for that. But David was also at the University of Miami in the jazz department. We did not know that we were both ending up in the same university. We had no idea that this was happening to us. So when I got there, and maybe it was because I had sort of become familiar with some of the people during that summer, during the youth jazz band concerts, maybe other things were kind of working themselves out for me. But I sustained this whole classical thing for the entire time I went to the University of Miami. But in the end it was like the beginning of my sophomore year, I really wanted to do this jazz thing but they didn’t have a curriculum for jazz singers. So they allowed me, Jerry Coker, they had a jazz department and the head of the classical department allowed me to go into the study but I had to do both, so I had this double music major. So now I’m staying in the classical but I’m now adding courses that had to do with composition, jazz arranging, improvisation, and they really treated me that way. In other words I just — my instrument was voice you see. So when it came time to improvise it wasn’t like they said okay do that on the piano. But now I’m taking jazz piano courses, I’m taking all these jazz courses and I’m staying in the classical department and I did both for the entire time. And I graduated as a jazz major. The curriculum for the jazz vocalist was established about three years after I left. So I kind of initiated this program without really, kind of having an intention to do so. But that’s kind of that little space in time where it really was a natural course of events. I think the reason that I was allowed to do this was because a lot of the jazz classmates that many of whom you’d know if I called their names you would know them, they would ask me to do their songs that they had to write for that class assignment or, “Can you sing — I wrote some lyrics for this Carmen, would you mind doing this tune for me?” You know. And the cool thing about it was while I had a little familiarity along the standards, this is an original idea — sing this new song that my classmate wrote. I couldn’t run to the library and find a version of it and kind of learn it based on the other vocalist’s rendition you see? I actually had to learn it and get inside the tune and perform it. So I was kind of forced to hear my own take on something. I was kind of in that place where it’s the other composer’s idea that I’m working with on this new song that I’m kind of helping him — he or she to realize what has been written. So that was kind of the osmosis part I think.
